uni-vlsi-core.title: VLSI and Embedded Systems core
uni-vlsi-core.description: Digital design, Verilog code-reading, CMOS fundamentals, embedded C and microcontroller peripherals for B.Tech ECE/VLSI learners, with numericals and code labs. Study companion; topics commonly taught in Indian B.Tech programmes.

courses.title: Digital design: number systems, Boolean algebra and timing
courses.summary: Two's complement, Boolean simplification, synchronous timing limits and counters.

scenes.text: A firmware intern stores −13 in an 8-bit register and reads it back as unsigned.
She wonders why she sees 243.

steps.title: Method
steps.body: Write +13 in binary, invert every bit, add 1. Range of n-bit two's complement is −2ⁿ⁻¹ to 2ⁿ⁻¹ − 1.

steps.title: Mistake
steps.body: The same bit pattern means different numbers when interpreted signed or unsigned.

activity.prompt: What unsigned decimal value does the 8-bit two's complement pattern of −13 represent?

You simplify a redundant term.

steps.title: Absorption
steps.body: Useful identity: **A + A'B = A + B**. Also A + AB = A and A(A + B) = A.

steps.title: Tools
steps.body: K-maps handle up to about 4–5 variables; synthesis tools use Quine–McCluskey and heuristics.

activity.prompt: Complete the identity.

options: any gate can be built from it

scenes.text: A register-to-register path has clock-to-Q 0.5 ns, logic 3.2 ns and setup 0.3 ns.
The lead asks how fast the clock can go.

steps.title: Constraint
steps.body: **Tclk ≥ tcq + tlogic + tsu** (ignoring clock skew).

steps.title: Hold
steps.body: Hold violations cannot be fixed by slowing the clock; delay must be added to the data path.

scenes.text: A board has a 25.6 MHz oscillator but a sensor needs a 100 kHz timebase.
You divide with an 8-bit counter.

steps.title: Division
steps.body: Bit k of a binary counter toggles at f/2^(k+1). The MSB of an n-bit counter runs at f/2ⁿ.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: 25.6 MHz / 256 = 100 kHz at bit 7.

steps.title: Real designs
steps.body: FPGAs use clock-enable ticks instead of derived clocks to avoid skew issues.

courses.title: Verilog reading: combinational and sequential blocks
courses.summary: Read and complete short Verilog descriptions: assign, mux, always blocks and register counting.

scenes.text: A fresher at a design house in Bengaluru writes her first module.
It must implement y = a AND b.

steps.title: Continuous assignment
steps.body: `assign` drives a wire continuously. Operators: & (AND), | (OR), ^ (XOR), ~ (NOT).

steps.title: Module
Mistake
steps.body: & is bitwise; && is logical. For single bits they match, for vectors they do not.

activity.prompt: module and2(input a, input b, output y); assign y = a ___ b; endmodule

scenes.text: A mux picks one of two inputs.
You finish the ternary expression.

steps.title: Ternary
steps.body: `assign y = sel ? b : a;` means y = b when sel = 1, else a.

steps.title: Truth table
steps.body: sel=0 → y=a; sel=1 → y=b.

steps.title: Synthesis
steps.body: A ternary on single bits maps to a mux cell.

activity.prompt: Complete so that sel = 1 selects b.

scenes.text: A register samples d on the rising clock edge.
You fill the sensitivity list.

steps.title: Sequential block
steps.body: `always @(posedge clk) q <= d;` infers a positive-edge D flip-flop. Use non-blocking `<=` in clocked blocks.

steps.title: With reset
steps.body:
always @(posedge clk or posedge rst)
  if (rst) q <= 1'b0; else q <= d;

steps.title: Mistake
steps.body: Mixing blocking and non-blocking assignments in one block causes simulation–synthesis mismatches.

activity.prompt: Complete the sensitivity list for a rising-edge flip-flop.

quiz.q: reg in Verilog always means a physical register
options: no, it depends on the block

scenes.text: A 4-bit up-counter runs on a 50 MHz clock in an FPGA.
Its terminal count drives a heartbeat signal; how fast does it roll over?

steps.title: Count
steps.body: reg [3:0] cnt; always @(posedge clk) cnt <= cnt + 1; infers 4 flip-flops and an incrementer. It takes 2⁴ = 16 cycles to wrap.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Period = 20 ns; 16 cycles = 320 ns.

steps.title: Practice
steps.body: A 26-bit counter at 50 MHz wraps in about 1.34 s.

activity.prompt: A 4-bit counter increments every clock of a 50 MHz clock. Time for a full wrap (16 cycles)?

courses.title: CMOS fundamentals: current, power, noise margin and delay
courses.summary: Square-law MOSFET current, dynamic power, noise margins and Elmore RC delay.

scenes.text: A layout engineer chooses W/L = 10 for an NMOS pull-down.
She estimates its drive current.

steps.title: Square law
steps.body: In saturation: **ID = ½ μnCox (W/L)(VGS − Vt)²** (long-channel approximation).

steps.title: Short channel
steps.body: Modern nodes show velocity saturation, so the dependence on overdrive is closer to linear.

activity.prompt: μnCox = 200 µA/V², W/L = 10, VGS = 1.0 V, Vt = 0.4 V. Saturation current?

steps.title: Formula
steps.body: **P = α C V² f**.

steps.title: Lever

courses.title: Embedded C: bit manipulation and buffers
courses.summary: Set, clear and count bits, and implement a circular buffer in short C programs.

lessons.title: Lab: Set a bit in a register

scenes.text: An output register bit 3 drives an LED.
You must set it without disturbing other bits.

steps.title: Set
steps.body: `reg |= (1u << n);` sets bit n and leaves others unchanged.

steps.title: Mistake
steps.body: Using `=` instead of `|=` overwrites the whole register.

activity.prompt: Set bit 3 in x and print the result as a decimal integer.

quiz.q: volatile on a register tells the compiler
options: value may change outside the program

scenes.text: Bit 2 of a control register enables an interrupt.
You must clear only that bit.

steps.title: Clear
steps.body: `reg &= ~(1u << n);` clears bit n.

steps.title: Toggle
steps.body: `reg ^= (1u << n);` toggles a bit.

activity.prompt: Clear bit 2 of x (starts as 0xFF) and print it as decimal.

scenes.text: A sensor frame 0xB5 must have its set bits counted for parity.
You write a loop.

steps.title: Loop
steps.body: Shift right and test the LSB: `count += x & 1; x >>= 1;`.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: 0xB5 = 10110101 has five 1s.

steps.title: Faster
steps.body: Kernighan's trick: `x &= x - 1` removes the lowest set bit each step.

activity.prompt: Count the 1 bits in 0xB5 and print the count.

scenes.text: A serial port writes bytes into a 4-slot ring buffer faster than the main loop reads.
Old data is overwritten when full.

steps.title: Ring buffer
steps.body: Write at `buf[head]` then `head = (head + 1) % N`.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Write 10..15 into 4 slots: final contents 14, 15, 12, 13; sum = 54.

steps.title: Interrupts
steps.body: If an ISR and main code share head/tail, use volatile and protect multi-step updates.

activity.prompt: Write the values 10 to 15 into a 4-element ring buffer (overwriting old ones) and print the sum of the buffer.

quiz.q: Full vs empty ambiguity is resolved with
options: a count or a spare slot

courses.title: Microcontroller peripherals: UART, timers and ADC
courses.summary: Baud-rate divisors, timer overflow periods, ADC resolution and voltage conversion in C.
outcomes: Convert ADC to millivolts in C

scenes.text: A 16 MHz AVR-style board prints rubbish at 9600 baud.
You recompute the baud register.

steps.title: Formula
steps.body: For normal-speed UART with 16× oversampling: **UBRR = f_cpu/(16×baud) − 1**.

steps.title: Error
steps.body: Rounding gives a small baud error; keep it under about 2%.

activity.prompt: f_cpu = 16 MHz, baud 9600, 16× oversampling. UBRR (round to integer)?

scenes.text: An 8-bit timer runs from a 16 MHz clock with a /64 prescaler.
You want the overflow interval.

steps.title: Tick
steps.body: Tick = prescaler/f_cpu; overflow time = counts × tick.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Tick = 64/16 MHz = 4 µs; 256 ticks = 1.024 ms.

steps.title: Compare mode
steps.body: Output-compare registers give exact intervals.

activity.prompt: 16 MHz clock, prescaler 64, 8-bit timer. Overflow period?

scenes.text: A 10-bit ADC with 5 V reference reads a knob at mid-scale.
You predict the count.

steps.title: Resolution
steps.body: **counts = Vin/Vref × 2ⁿ** (full scale 2ⁿ−1 in many parts). Resolution (LSB) = Vref/2ⁿ.

steps.title: Noise
steps.body: Averaging samples reduces noise.

activity.prompt: 10-bit ADC, Vref = 5 V, Vin = 2.5 V. Count?

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone – ADC to millivolts in C

scenes.text: The firmware reads an ADC count of 768 on a 10-bit, 5000 mV reference.
You convert with integer arithmetic only.

steps.title: Integer maths
steps.body: mV = adc × 5000 / 1024. Multiply first to keep precision; use 32-bit intermediates.

steps.title: Overflow
steps.body: On a 16-bit int, 768×5000 overflows; cast to a 32-bit type.

activity.prompt: Convert adc = 768 to millivolts (Vref 5000 mV, 10-bit) using 32-bit integers and print it.
